home_info.title: Exploring how plants, microbes and insects interact across ecosystems.
home_info.lede: Ecobiome Laboratory is an interdisciplinary research group combining molecular biology, microbial ecology and entomology to understand the ecological web that connects three kingdoms of life.
home_info.mission_body:
Plants do not grow, defend themselves, or reproduce in isolation. Every root is embedded in a community of bacteria and fungi; every leaf is a surface that insects taste, feed on, and are deterred by.

Our researchers combine molecular biology, microbial ecology and field-based entomology to ask how plant health, soil microbiomes and insect communities influence one another — and what this means for ecosystem resilience, agriculture and climate adaptation.

Every project we run moves between three settings: the open field, where interactions are first observed; the growth chamber, where conditions can be controlled; and the molecular laboratory, where mechanisms are confirmed.

home_about.title: Why we study plants, microbes and insects together.
home_about.vision_title: A more complete picture of ecological interaction
home_about.vision_text: We envision a research community that studies plants, microbes and insects together rather than as separate disciplines — because in nature, they never act alone. Our long-term vision is to build one of the field's most integrative datasets connecting molecular microbiome data with insect ecology across the same study systems.
home_about.history_title: How the laboratory came to be
home_about.history_text: Ecobiome Laboratory was established by a small group of plant biologists and entomologists who shared a frustration: microbiome studies rarely accounted for insect activity, and insect ecology studies rarely accounted for the microbial state of the host plant. We favour long-term, repeated sampling over one-off snapshots, and paired molecular and field data over either alone.
home_about.quote: Every leaf we study carries a microbial community and a history of insect encounters. Understanding a plant in isolation only tells part of the story — our laboratory exists to tell the rest of it.
home_about.quote_author: Dr. Alexander Karimov, Principal Investigator, Ecobiome Laboratory (demo profile)

research_areas.title: Plant–Microbe Interactions
research_areas.summary: We study how root-associated and leaf-surface microbial communities influence plant nutrition, growth and immune signalling, and how plants in turn select and shape their microbial partners.
questions: How does root exudate chemistry recruit specific bacterial taxa?
Do beneficial microbes prime plant immune responses against pathogens?
How stable are plant–microbe associations across generations?
research_areas.methods: 16S/ITS amplicon sequencing, gnotobiotic plant assays, confocal microscopy of root colonisation.
research_areas.current_focus: Rhizosphere recruitment in Arabidopsis thaliana under nutrient stress.

research_areas.title: Plant–Insect Interactions
research_areas.summary: This area examines the chemical and physical dialogue between plants and insects — from herbivore feeding and induced defences to pollination and insect-vectored microbes.
questions: How do herbivore-induced plant volatiles affect neighbouring plants and predators?
What role do insects play in dispersing plant-associated microbes?
How does leaf chemistry mediate insect host-plant choice?
research_areas.methods: Volatile organic compound (VOC) analysis, choice-assay bioassays, field herbivory surveys.
research_areas.current_focus: Herbivore-induced volatiles and microbiome shifts in Quercus robur canopies.
research_areas.related_projects: Insect Biodiversity Atlas, Forest Ecosystem Interactions.

research_areas.title: Soil Microbiomes
research_areas.summary: We characterise the composition and function of soil bacterial and fungal communities across agricultural and natural land uses, and how they respond to management practices.
questions: How does land management alter soil microbial diversity and function?
Which taxa are reliable indicators of soil health?
How resilient are soil microbiomes to disturbance?
research_areas.methods: Shotgun metagenomics, soil enzyme assays, long-term plot monitoring.
research_areas.current_focus: Comparing shaded and unshaded coffee agroecosystem soils.
research_areas.related_projects: Coffee Agroecosystem Research, Soil Microbiome Dynamics.

research_areas.title: Biodiversity & Ecosystems
research_areas.summary: This area quantifies species diversity and interaction networks — plant, microbial and insect — across natural and managed landscapes, tracking how diversity relates to ecosystem stability.
questions: How does habitat fragmentation affect interaction network structure?
Does higher plant diversity buffer insect outbreak risk?
What indicators best capture ecosystem-level biodiversity change?
research_areas.methods: Transect surveys, pitfall and light trapping, network analysis.
research_areas.current_focus: Cataloguing insect diversity across a forest–farmland gradient.

research_areas.title: Climate & Plant Health
research_areas.summary: We investigate how shifting temperature and precipitation patterns alter plant disease dynamics, microbiome composition and pest pressure.
questions: Does warming shift the balance between beneficial and pathogenic microbes?
How does drought stress alter plant susceptibility to herbivory?
Can microbiome engineering buffer climate-driven disease risk?
research_areas.methods: Controlled-environment chamber experiments, drought-stress trials, disease incidence monitoring.
research_areas.current_focus: Drought-linked disease susceptibility in temperate tree seedlings.

research_areas.title: Molecular Ecology
research_areas.summary: This area applies genomic and transcriptomic tools to understand adaptation, gene flow, and functional traits underlying plant, microbial and insect interactions.
questions: Which genes underlie plant recognition of beneficial versus pathogenic microbes?
How much local adaptation exists in microbial partners across sites?
What functional traits distinguish resilient microbial communities?
research_areas.methods: RNA-seq, comparative genomics, population genetic analysis.
research_areas.current_focus: Comparative transcriptomics of oak immune response to combined stress.

research_areas.title: Spatial Ecology
research_areas.summary: We examine how interactions vary across space — from microhabitat differences within a single tree canopy to landscape-scale gradients between forest and farmland.
questions: How does distance from forest edge affect insect community composition?
Do microbiome gradients track landscape connectivity?
What spatial scale best predicts interaction network stability?
research_areas.methods: GIS-based landscape analysis, spatially nested sampling designs, remote sensing.
research_areas.current_focus: Mapping herbivory intensity across a forest-edge gradient.

research_areas.title: Evolutionary Ecology
research_areas.summary: This area studies how co-evolutionary pressures between plants, microbes and insects shape trait diversification over time, using both field observation and comparative analysis.
questions: Do plant defence traits co-evolve with specific insect herbivore lineages?
How stable are mutualisms with microbial partners over evolutionary time?
What role does geographic isolation play in trait divergence?
research_areas.methods: Comparative phylogenetics, common-garden experiments, trait-mapping analysis.
research_areas.current_focus: Co-evolutionary signatures in oak defence-chemistry variation.

projects.study_system: Temperate tree seedlings (Quercus robur, Fagus sylvatica)
projects.outcomes: A predictive model of climate-linked disease risk

projects.title: Forest Ecosystem Interactions
projects.overview: Our flagship project tracking individual oak trees across seasons for leaf microbiome, root fungal associates and insect herbivory.
projects.question: How do microbial and herbivore pressures on the same host tree interact over time?
projects.objectives: Build a longitudinal, individual-tree-level dataset linking microbiome and herbivory
projects.methods: Repeated leaf and soil sampling, VOC analysis, insect surveys
projects.study_system: Quercus robur across six forest plots
projects.outcomes: A seasonal model of tree-level microbiome–herbivore dynamics

projects.overview: Comparing soil and canopy biodiversity between shaded and unshaded Coffea arabica plantations.
projects.question: Does shade-grown coffee support richer soil microbiomes and insect communities than sun-grown coffee?
projects.objectives: Compare microbial and insect diversity across management types; assess yield trade-offs
projects.methods: Paired-plot sampling, metagenomics, insect transect surveys

news.title: Autumn sampling campaign begins at the oak-forest field site
news.label: Fieldwork
news.excerpt: Our field team has started the seasonal leaf and soil sampling round used to track microbiome shifts through autumn senescence, continuing the Forest Ecosystem Interactions project.
news.body:
Our field research team has begun the autumn round of the Forest Ecosystem Interactions project's seasonal sampling schedule. This is the fourth consecutive year the same set of marked oak (Quercus robur) trees across six forest plots has been sampled at this time of year, allowing the team to track how leaf-surface microbial communities shift as trees move into senescence.

Each sampling visit follows a standardised protocol: leaf discs are collected from three canopy heights per tree for microbiome profiling, paired soil cores are taken from the root zone, and a structured visual survey records signs of insect herbivory on the same branches sampled in the previous season.

"Autumn is one of the more interesting windows in this dataset," said Dr. Madina Rahimova, who coordinates the field programme. "Leaf chemistry is changing rapidly as the tree reallocates resources, and we consistently see shifts in both the fungal community and the insects still active on the canopy at this time."

Samples collected during this campaign will be processed in the laboratory's molecular biology and microscopy facilities over the coming weeks, with amplicon sequencing results expected by early winter. The resulting dataset will feed into the project's ongoing model linking microbiome shifts to seasonal herbivore pressure.

The campaign is expected to run through early October, weather permitting, and will be followed by the project's regular winter dormant-season baseline sampling.
